generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, feedback in the School of Sport arrives in more forms than a single grade: a mark, comments on your clinical reasoning, a completed rubric against the module criteria, a few spoken words after a practical, even a comparison with a marked exemplar. Whatever form it takes, the useful step is the same: work out what it is asking you to do differently in the next case study or report, and treat that as the point of it rather than the verdict. Your modules deliberately pair feedback with feedforward, so the comment is meant to carry into what you do next.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy and rehabilitation students get the same comment on a draft case study: You describe the injury and the treatment well, but you do not evaluate your clinical reasoning.

Tom reads the comment at face value, as a small complaint rather than an instruction, and misses the action it is asking for. Nothing changes in how he writes, so in the next case study the same problem appears and the same comment comes back: the mistake has simply been repeated.

Amara works out the action behind the comment: it is asking for a judgement about her reasoning, not more description. She plans the next case study around weighing the assessment findings, the treatment choice and the evidence base against the outcome, and writes to that. The next case study evaluates the reasoning, and the comment does not return.

Both read the same words. Only Amara read the action behind them and acted on it. That is what feedback is for in the School of Sport: it tells you what to do differently, and acting on it is how your work improves from one report to the next.
generatedProse.summary: Feedback is the comments and insights that tell you how to improve, and in the School of Sport it arrives in many forms, not just a mark. You can now recognise those forms, and, the skill that makes feedback worth having, work out the action a comment is really asking you to take. Reading the action behind the words, and feeding it forward into the next case study or report, is what turns feedback into better work.

check.body: A tutor writes on your sport therapy case study: 'This is mostly description of the injury and treatment; I would like to see more of your own evaluation of your clinical reasoning.' What is this comment asking you to do?

items.text: Weigh your assessment findings and treatment choices against the evidence and show how sound your reasoning is, rather than just reporting it.
Add more description to be thorough.
Change the case to an easier injury.

feedback.correct: That's right. The comment asks for evaluation: weighing your findings, choices and evidence and judging how sound your reasoning is, not more description or more words.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. The comment contrasts description with evaluation, so look for the option that asks you to judge, not to report.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The comment asks you to evaluate: to weigh your assessment findings and treatment choices against the evidence and show how sound your reasoning is. More words, more description or an easier case would each miss the action it is pointing to.
